senses.gloss:
ādhāracakra
(‘supporting psychic centre’)
------------------------------------------
See CAKRAS and MŪLĀDHĀRA.

ādhāra
(‘support’)
------------------------------------------
One of the questions discussed frequently in Hindu metaphysical works is the relationship between God, the creator and the created world. Most of them subscribe to the view that God creates the world, sustains and supports it and dissolves it at the end of a cycle of च्रेअतिओन्. The created world cannot exist unless it is supported and sustained by him. He is thus the आधार (the ground and the support) and the world itself is ādheya (‘that which is supported’). The relationship that subsists between them is called ‘ādhara-ādheya-भाव.’ The relationship that exists between the ground and a jar kept on it gives us some idea of this ‘ādhāra-ādheya-भाव.’
In the works on योग, the word is used to indicate certain centres in the body like the navel, the heart or the middle of the eyebrows which act as supports for meditation or प्राण (life-force).
In Sanskrit grammar the word is used to indicate the sense of the locative case.

ādhāraśilā
(‘support-stone’)
------------------------------------------
Belief in God and putting up structures to worship him or to pray to him seems to be a common trait of human beings irrespective of their geographical boundaries or differences of culture. There are evidences to show that the Hindu places of worship, called devālayas (temples, houses of God), have been existing since very ancient times. These devālayas are highly symbolic and attempt at unravelling this symbology, in concrete terms, have resulted in a regular science and art of temple construction. Apart from the usual foundation laid to support the superstructure of the temple, these works on temple construction insist on the laying of the आधारशिला or support-stone below the floor of the गर्भगृह (sanctum sanctorum).
In the middle of the site for the गर्भगृह, where the idol will be installed, the ground is excavated to a pre-determined depth. A number of articles are ceremonially fixed therein, one after another, with appropriate mantras. (See ṢAḌĀDHĀRA-PRATIṢṬHĀ.) Of these, the आधारशिला is the first to be fixed, and at the lowest level, as the base or support. It is a square block of granite or any other hard stone, of specific dimensions. On it are placed the other articles like the pot called निधिकुम्भ and the lotuses of stone and metal.
According to one of the interpretations of temple symbolism, the temple represents the body of the योगि (the spiritual aspirant practising योग) with all the चक्रस् (centres of psychic power). The आधार-śilā, then, stands for the मूलाधार-चक्र (the lowest centre).
See also CAKRAS.

adharma
(‘unrighteousness’)
------------------------------------------
Among the pairs of words used often by the Hindu scriptures, the pair ‘dharma-अधर्म’ is perhaps the most recurrent. Since the etymological definition of ‘dharma’ is ‘that which supports and sustains,’ all that attempts to destroy or oppose or reverse this process of supporting and sustaining comes within the purview of the word ‘adharma.’ If धर्म is the straight path that leads to abhyu-daya (well-being and prosperity) and niśśreyasa (spiritual perfection), अधर्म is the crooked path that leads away from both. If धर्म indicates actions and duties, ritualistic or otherwise, which are in conformity with the teachings of the śāstras (holy scriptures) and ācāryas (spiritual and religious leaders), and not antagonistic to सम्प्रदाय (customs and traditions), अधर्म stands for all errors of omission and commission.
In practice however, the word is more frequently used in the sense of unrighteous deeds and conduct resulting in sin. For instance, telling lies, stealing, cheating, अदुल्तेर्य् and committing such other forbidden acts and crimes are अधर्म. Dereliction of duties and not discharging the responsibilities one is entrusted with, are अधर्म. Performing such acts as are not prescribed for one—for e.g., a ब्राह्मण taking to arms or agriculture even though there is no urgency or emergency—is also considered अधर्म.
The personified अधर्म, in the mythological lore, is said to have हिṁसा (violence) as his wife, अनृत (falsehood) as his son, and nikṛti (deceit) as his daughter. Māyā (delusion), bhaya (fear), vedanā (torment), नरक (hell), दुःख (sorrow) and मृत्यु (death) are the other offsprings coming in that lineage (vide Viṣṇupurāṇa 1.7). Though the details of such lists may vary, the purport is clear: अधर्म is at the root of all our fears, troubles and sufferings.
In Jaina metaphysics, अधर्म is considered to be a द्रव्य (substance) responsible for restful state and immobility of things.
See also DHARMA and PĀPA.
